rows.mechanism: Trees and live fences carry livestock through drought as a fodder reserve: trees were the main source of animal feed and milk production for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought, and live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species supply high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. During drought, understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade, silvopastures are credited with better water infiltration rates, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
rows.conditionality: The Zambian, US and Sahelian parkland units come from agro-pastoral systems, and the US silvopasture unit is high-income evidence that names infiltration rather than a drought outcome [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]; the understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, as tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The Ethiopian unit is a stakeholder rating of a bundled sustainable land management programme (terracing, bunds, area closure, small-scale irrigation, agroforestry), so its effect is not attributable to agroforestry alone [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4], a Nigerian model study, used as an income proxy, found no significant impact on agroforestry household net revenues under a simulated warmer, drier climate [ev_household_income_watts22_14], and the Kenyan FMNR unit is a compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. Against the benefit, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition; it is a cited, high-income cropping result applied here by default [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper, and the parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1].

at_a_glance.headline: low · high
at_a_glance.statement_short: Agroforestry under drought (agro pastoral): low mitigation (high confidence; 10 units, 9 sources) · harm reported in 1 source

rows.mechanism: In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also share deep water and act as a fodder reserve: hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, millet with the shrub Guiera senegalensis in the Sahel produced over 900% more biomass under water stress, trees were the main source of feed and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought, and in Senegal's sylvopastoral zone tree leaves, fruits and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle diet before the rains [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. In an induced drought in eastern Canada only the monocrop lost yield, agroforestry biomass in the Brazilian semi-arid varied far less over 4 years than conventional systems, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. In Cañas, Costa Rica, cattle on pasture with high tree density gained 2 to 5% more weight in the dry season than those on low-cover pasture, attributed partly to longer grazing and rumination under reduced heat stress [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Live fences of species such as Gliricidia sepium and Leucaena leucocephala supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. For shaded cocoa and coffee: in a throughfall-exclusion experiment in Ghana, cocoa dry bean yield was 12 to 45% higher under shade than in full sun at every level of rainwater suppression [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1]; in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly positive for coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11].
rows.conditionality: The class comes from the sub-practice vote, not the pooled units: the regeneration-on-farmland, planted silvoarable and silvopastoral cells read as benefits, while the linear-boundary and shaded perennial-crop cells are conflicting. Trade-offs pull the other way: tree–maize competition for soil water in Kenya can lead to crop failure, and a Senegal review finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought, with some studies reporting higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, since tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Kenyan household link to perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. Several units are proxies, bundled or rated rather than measured: a Nigerian model found no significant drought impact on household net revenues, the Ethiopian rating covers a whole sustainable land management package, the Canadian and US units are high-income evidence, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating [ev_household_income_watts22_14, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. A cited temperate finding of greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years adds to the counter-evidence, the German soil-water difference was not significant everywhere and is high-income evidence, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper, and the parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Costa Rican liveweight result is high-income evidence from a review citing an earlier study, and it measures dry-season weight gain rather than drought losses [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure; the same study reports its normal-season gain separately, so this hazard-year gain is not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In shaded cocoa and coffee the evidence is split: reviews cite that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms, that drought caused greater water loss in cacao agroforests than in open-sun cacao because trees and cacao both transpire, and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_9, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]; and in the Ghana experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2]. These harm findings are second-hand readings in reviews. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2].
rows.statement: agroforestry slightly reduces the impact of drought in ARG, BFA, BRA, CAN, COL, CRI, DEU, ETH, GHA, HND, KEN, MEX, MLI, NER, NGA, NIC, PER, SEN, USA, ZMB; the measured evidence also includes no-benefit or reversal results under drought, which discount the class; only 8 of 34 units in this direction say how big the effect is, so the class is capped at moderate; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 3 sources — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, medium agreement → high confidence; transfer: in_context). at_a_glance.headline: moderate · high
at_a_glance.statement_short: Agroforestry under drought (all farming systems): moderate mitigation (high confidence; 44 units, 24 sources) · harm reported in 3 sources
at_a_glance.family_vote_line: cross-family +1 · boundary ± · silvoarable +2 · regeneration +4 · shaded ± · silvopastoral +2

rows.mechanism: On rainfed cropland the evidence divides on whether trees add water the crop can use or compete with the crop for it. Hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, and in the Sahel millet intercropped with the shrub Guiera senegalensis produced over 900% more biomass under water stress [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system, and during drought understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]; the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2].
rows.conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland holds the stronger result and reads as a benefit throughout: Sahelian parkland trees make deep soil moisture available to crop roots, the FMNR compiler rates drought impacts as mitigated, Quesungual crops withstood the 1997 drought, and Ethiopian wheat under Faidherbia albida out-yielded open-field wheat in the El Niño year, a hazard-year result kept apart from the study's normal-season gain [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. On the conflicting side, planted silvoarable systems pair gains (the Canadian induced drought, the Sahelian millet–Guiera result, the Ethiopian programme rating, German alley-cropping soil water) with a reversal, Kenyan maize under Grevillea robusta, where competition for limited soil water delayed flowering and can lead to crop failure [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]; and boundary plantings pair a live-fence fodder role in drought with greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years and a Senegal review that finds no consensus on windbreak hedges in drought [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. What separates the sides in the units' own words is whether tree roots reach moisture the crop cannot, or compete with the crop for limited soil water close to the trees. The understorey drought-year result and the Nigerian income model sit outside the voting sub-practices: the understorey benefit reverses under normal rainfall, and the income model found no significant drought effect [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The Canadian result is high-income temperate evidence, the Ethiopian unit rates a bundled sustainable land management programme, the live-fence fodder unit is a pantropical review, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant at all positions and is high-income evidence, and the Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
rows.statement: agroforestry moderately reduces the impact of drought in CAN, DEU, ETH, HND, KEN, NGA, SEN; the measured evidence also includes no-benefit or reversal results under drought, which discount the class; only 3 of 10 units in this direction say how big the effect is, so the class is capped at moderate; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 2 sources — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, high agreement → very_high confidence; transfer: in_context). CLASS SET BY SUB-PRACTICE VOTE: the family rows disagree (linear_boundary=conflicting_evidence, planted_silvoarable=conflicting_evidence, regeneration_farmland=very_high), so the roll-up states conflicting evidence rather than the pooled moderate.
rows.pool_note: This row draws on 14 evidence unit(s) from 12 source(s); the weighting counts sources, not units, so several findings from one paper do not multiply its say.

family_vote.rule: family rows vote with weight sqrt(n_sources); dissent >= 0.33 of signed weight -> conflicting_evidence (Pete 2026-10-19, rollup_family_honesty B)

at_a_glance.headline: CONFLICTING
at_a_glance.statement_short: Agroforestry under drought (cropping rainfed): evidence conflicts — sub-practices disagree (boundary ± · silvoarable ± · regeneration +4) · harm reported in 2 sources

rows.mechanism: In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14]. In the Brazilian semi-arid, agroforestry biomass productivity varied far less over 4 years than conventional systems, which the source attributes mainly to water availability, and live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species carry livestock through dry periods with high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
rows.conditionality: The Kenyan household units are a single study of survey and farmer-interview evidence, and the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. The Ethiopian unit is a stakeholder rating of a bundled sustainable land management programme (terracing, bunds, area closure, small-scale irrigation, agroforestry), so its effect is not attributable to agroforestry alone, and a Nigerian model study, used as an income proxy, found no significant impact on agroforestry household net revenues under a simulated warmer, drier climate [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Nyando units rest on income and coping strategies as proxies for drought impact, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported rather than measured [ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. Earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years, a high-income cropping result applied here by default [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
rows.statement: agroforestry slightly reduces the impact of drought in BRA, ETH, HND, KEN, NGA; the measured evidence also includes no-benefit or reversal results under drought, which discount the class; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 1 source — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, high agreement → very_high confidence; transfer: in_context).

rows.mechanism: In Senegal's sylvopastoral zone, tree leaves, fruits and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle diet and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diet in the run-up to the rains, and live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species supply high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. During drought, understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. In Cañas, Costa Rica, cattle on pasture with high tree density gained 2 to 5% more weight in the dry season than those on low-cover pasture, attributed partly to longer grazing and rumination under reduced heat stress [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
rows.conditionality: The class follows the sub-practice vote, which lifts the pooled result: silvopasture holds the stronger result, with forage held steady and cattle better fed through drought, milk rising in Colombia in the lowest-rainfall year in several decades, and higher dry-season weight gain in Costa Rica, while regeneration-based farmland (the Senegal tree-fodder unit, the Kenyan FMNR rating and the Honduran Quesungual result) reads weaker, so the NbS-level class sits at the silvopastoral reading [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. Because the stronger side is mostly earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews and a CATIE edited volume, the lift rests on secondary reporting rather than new measurement. The live-fence fodder unit, the shelterbelt dry-year loss, the review statement on understorey yields, the Nigerian model and the Ethiopian programme rating belong to sub-practices or cross-cutting evidence that has no family row of its own in this cell, so they shape agreement but not the class [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_household_income_watts22_14, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. The Senegal fodder unit and the Latin American silvopastoral units come from pastoral rangeland systems; the rest are applied to pastoral rangeland by default [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. The Ethiopian unit is a stakeholder rating of a bundled sustainable land management programme (terracing, bunds, area closure, small-scale irrigation, agroforestry), so its effect is not attributable to agroforestry alone, and a Nigerian model study, used as an income proxy, found no significant impact on agroforestry household net revenues under a simulated warmer, drier climate [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The FMNR unit is a compiler rating, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. Earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition, a high-income cropping result applied here by default [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The Latin American silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Costa Rican liveweight result is high-income evidence from a review citing an earlier study, and it measures dry-season weight gain rather than drought losses [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

rows.mechanism: Evidence that trees lessen drought impacts in tree-crop systems comes from shaded cocoa and coffee and from general agroforestry reports. For shaded cocoa and coffee: in a throughfall-exclusion experiment in Ghana, cocoa dry bean yield was 12 to 45% higher under shade than in full sun at every level of rainwater suppression [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1]; in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly positive for coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. A review adds that under normal rainfall tree shade can lower understorey crop yields, while during drought those yields can be higher than in an open system, even in intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the particularly severe 1997 drought while non-adopters suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]; live fences supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]; the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]; and in Ethiopia's sustainable land management programme, income from commercial agroforestry was named as one option that reduced drought vulnerability in some communities [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].
rows.conditionality: No-benefit and harm findings discount the class. In the Ghana experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on cocoa yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced decline; the Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in extreme climate shocks; on Bahia cocoa farms drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover; and a model cited in a review found no significant impact on Nigerian agroforestry household net revenues under a simulated warmer, drier climate [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The harm findings are all second-hand readings in reviews: under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms, that drought caused greater water loss in cacao agroforests than in open-sun cacao because trees and cacao both transpire, and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_9, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8], and earlier work cited in a German alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. Only those units and the cocoa and coffee review statements record a tree-perennial system; the Honduran, live-fence, FMNR, Ethiopian, Nigerian, understorey and shelterbelt units record none and are applied here by default [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_household_income_watts22_14, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The Ethiopian unit is a stakeholder rating of a bundled sustainable land management package (terracing, bunds, area closure, small-scale irrigation, agroforestry), not attributable to agroforestry alone [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]; the FMNR unit is a compiler rating; and the Honduran observation is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

rows.mechanism: The silvopasture study in this cell compared silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest in Washington State, USA: silvopasture management reduced grass biomass, litter and duff depth, and the authors conclude that managing overstory, understory and grazing together can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5]. Rotational grazing removes understory biomass and herbaceous surface fuel, and the reduced, more variable overstory density has the potential to reduce fire frequency compared with other land uses [ev_t3_herbaceous_fuel_batcheler24_4, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. Rate of fire spread and burn severity correlate with litter and duff depth in this forest type, which is why the litter reduction matters for fire [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. Separately, a Kenyan compiler for farmer managed natural regeneration rates that tree cover can increase the risk of major wild fires, and that fire breaks should be considered for larger sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].
rows.conditionality: None of this evidence can set the class. Every comparison is against the unmanaged state, non-grazed managed forest, while this cell asks how silvopasture compares with the open pasture of an agro-pastoral system [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5, ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8]. Against treeless pasture the reading changes: introducing trees adds woody material, litter and duff that open pasture does not have, so having less fuel than a forest does not mean having less fuel than the pasture the practice replaces. Read against that comparator, the fire-spread correlation with litter and duff depth would point to added risk rather than a reduction [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. The study is also from a high-income US setting in the Interior Columbia Basin, outside the LIC/LMIC target; only select fuel types fell (1-, 10-, 100- and 1000-h fuels were similar between the management systems), and the fire-frequency statement is a potential effect, not a measurement [ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. What would fill the gap is a fire-risk comparison (fuel load, fire frequency or burn severity) of silvopasture against treeless pasture, ideally in an LIC/LMIC agro-pastoral system. The Kenyan WOCAT rating is carried but cannot set the class either: it is a practitioner judgement, not a measurement, and as the only evidence from a different source it sits below the evidence floor, which needs another independent source or a measured finding [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk]. rows.mechanism: In Vietnam, farms with trees were less affected by an extreme flood that caused heavy crop losses in the region [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11]. In Isiolo County, Kenya, households said trees planted in a line stop soil being swept away by water and named tree species useful during floods, and the study concludes that agroforestry builds livelihood resilience to floods; the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) adds that it mitigates the impact of annual floods on crops and settlements [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6, ev_t3_flood_erosion_table_quandt17_13, ev_t3_flood_conclusion_quandt17_11, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_507_2019_flood_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods, and some had fruit from their trees as their only steady food when other crops were underwater or washed away [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. A review also reports that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
rows.conditionality: The Vietnamese result is cited second-hand and the 40% figure in it is the regional crop loss, not the effect of trees [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11]. The Kenyan household units come from a single study of farmer interviews in a semi-arid area, the line-planting unit concerns soil erosion by water as a component of flood impact, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_507_2019_flood_impacts]. The Nyando flood units are farmer-reported, from interviews and focus groups, and enter through soil erosion and food supply as components of flood impact [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. The Mesoamerican coffee statement is a crop-specific, second-hand review citation with no country, income group or size recorded [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].

at_a_glance.headline: low · medium
at_a_glance.statement_short: Agroforestry under heat stress (agro pastoral): low mitigation (medium confidence; 9 units, 7 sources)

rows.mechanism: Measured cooling reaches crops: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, and lower heat load under Populus deltoides in India raised wheat grain yield by 6.8% [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. For cattle, shade from live fences reduces heat stress, giving a more comfortable environment and supporting reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3]. In a shade-by-drought experiment on cocoa in Ghana, sub-canopy temperatures were lower in shade than in full-sun plots [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. Reviews and syntheses report the same cooling more generally: over-storey shade moderates severe temperature (2–4°C) effects on understorey crops, tree shading can lower ambient temperature by 4°C and soil temperature by 6–10°C, agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress, shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise coffee yields, and shade trees produce microclimates that buffer temperature fluctuations [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3]. In Senegal's Ferlo, air temperature under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C to 42 °C outside, and access to the cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and so raises animal productivity [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. In cocoa and coffee, a pantropical synthesis found mean temperature lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures buffered in cocoa agroforestry against monocultures, a review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, and measurements in Costa Rican coffee found shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
rows.conditionality: Windbreak hedges in Senegal generally cause a slight temperature rise in the protected plots, with effects that vary by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. Most units report cooling or animal comfort, entering as components of heat-stress impact, and nearly all are reviews citing earlier studies. The yield and milk-production units apply to hot conditions only, and the German alley-cropping unit is high-income temperate evidence [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. The Ghanaian cocoa shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so it captures above-ground shading only and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. The shelterbelt cooling is a pooled meta-analysis result from upper-middle-income China, expressed as a modest percentage change in air temperature rather than a measured heat-stress loss [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The Ethiopian cooling was measured on farm, but its yield link is modelled, and the model's null without applied N is among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The IPCC chapter that says shade trees can ameliorate rising stand temperatures for arabica coffee adds in the same sentence that the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; they report temperature rather than heat-stress losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].

rows.mechanism: Measured cooling reaches crops: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, and lower heat load under Populus deltoides in India raised wheat grain yield by 6.8% [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. Tree shade lowers the temperature crops and animals experience: IPCC and other reviews state that agroforestry reduces ambient temperature and crop heat stress, with over-storey shade moderating severe temperature effects by 2–4°C and tree shading lowering air temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1].
rows.conditionality: Windbreak hedges in Senegal generally cause a slight temperature rise in the protected plots, with effects that vary by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The Ethiopian, German, Indian, Senegalese and Chinese units come from rainfed cropping, and the German unit is high-income temperate evidence; the yield gain applies to hot conditions only [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Most units are reviews citing earlier studies and report cooling, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. The shelterbelt cooling is a pooled meta-analysis result from upper-middle-income China, expressed as a modest percentage change in air temperature rather than a measured heat-stress loss [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The Ethiopian cooling was measured on farm, but its yield link is modelled, and the model's null without applied N is among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4].

rows.mechanism: For mixed systems with cattle, a Brazilian comparison found 20 to 100% reductions in areas at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals under agroforestry compared with monoculture, and live-fence shade is reported to reduce cattle heat stress, supporting reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]. For crops, shade buffers severe temperature effects on understorey crops and lowers ambient temperature by 4°C, and in Kenya shade trees are described as buffering temperature fluctuations [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1].

Only the Brazilian and Kenyan units are recorded as mixed crop-livestock; the others carry no or a different farming system and are applied by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. rows.mechanism: Silvopastoral and pasture trees cut cattle heat stress: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. For cattle, shade from live fences reduces heat stress, giving a more comfortable environment and supporting reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].
rows.conditionality: The Latin American silvopastoral units come from pastoral rangeland; the general reviews are applied here by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. Most units are reviews citing earlier studies, and the milk and weight-gain figures are associations with shade rather than measured heat-stress losses avoided [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].
rows.statement: agroforestry moderately reduces the impact of heat_stress in BRA, COL, CRI, CUB, MEX, NIC, PER; no measured evidence at severe or extreme heat_stress (robust evidence, high agreement → very_high confidence; transfer: adjacent).

rows.mechanism: Reviews report that tree shade buffers severe temperature effects on understorey crops and lowers ambient temperature by 4°C, that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress, and that shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise yields of crops like coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. Shade from live fences is reported to reduce cattle heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]. Shade over cocoa and coffee lowers the temperature the crop experiences. A pantropical synthesis of cocoa studies found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures are buffered compared with monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress, and the IPCC notes that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Measured on plots, shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee, and sub-canopy temperatures in a Ghanaian cocoa experiment were on average 1.5–3.1 °C lower in shade than in full sun [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1].
rows.conditionality: Only the cocoa and coffee units record a tree-perennial system; the general review statements are applied by default, and the cattle-shade units concern livestock [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. The Ghanaian cocoa shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so it captures above-ground shading only and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1]. Recorded countries include Cuba (upper-middle income), Ghana (lower-middle income) and Costa Rica (recorded as high income), and several units have no country or income group, so the transfer is classed adjacent, and all the review units rest on temperature buffering, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. The IPCC sentence that credits shade trees for coffee adds that the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].

rows.mechanism: Boundary and line plantings slow the wind: the zone of reduced wind speed typically extends 10 to 20 times tree height downwind, hedges protect sandy, poorly covered soils from wind erosion in Senegal, and live fences serve as windbreaks in India [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. Windbreaks are reported to raise wheat yields by 15 to 20% and to protect plants from winter desiccation, and a meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found wind speed 35.80% lower in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. The evidence about trees on farms in general points both ways: a review of smallholder agroforestry notes that trees on farm serve as windbreaks and shelterbelts and are used to rebuild property damaged during storms, while a Latin American adaptation review gives the planting of shade trees that damage existing infrastructure in storms as an example of increased vulnerability [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. A Kenyan study also states, citing Philpott et al. 2008, that trees can buffer crops from storms [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4]. That cited study, read directly, looked at hurricane-hit coffee in Soconusco, Chiapas, and found significant effects of vegetation management on landslides but not on coffee harvest lost, with all farms reporting yield losses between 18 and 40% [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].
rows.conditionality: The benefit side rests on windbreak function: boundary and line plantings slowing everyday wind and wind erosion, entering as components rather than measured storm or cyclone losses [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4, ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. The other side has two parts. The no-benefit finding is the Chiapas harvest result: after the hurricane, coffee harvest loss did not differ with vegetation management, so shade trees in coffee did not protect the crop in that study [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]; this shaded perennial-crop sub-practice therefore shows no mitigation and pulls against the windbreak families. The harm finding is a Latin American adaptation review's example of shade trees that damage existing infrastructure in storms, set against a smallholder review noting trees used as windbreaks and to rebuild storm-damaged property [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5, ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1]. The separator is design and placement: a windbreak laid out to shelter a field is a different thing from shade trees standing next to buildings or other infrastructure when a storm hits, and the evidence does not say how far the windbreak benefit holds once winds reach storm or cyclone strength. Most units are reviews or cited statements of earlier work; the wheat-yield unit gives no location [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7]. The Chinese shelterbelt result measures everyday wind speed in upper-middle-income China [ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. The Chiapas unit is crop-specific (coffee) from upper-middle-income Mexico and counts because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The Kenyan storm-buffer statement is a background citation of that same Chiapas study, not a measurement made in Kenya, and the study it cites does not show a harvest benefit [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].
rows.statement: agroforestry moderately reduces the impact of wind_cyclone in CHN, IND, KEN, MEX, SEN; the measured evidence also includes no-benefit or reversal results under wind_cyclone, which discount the class; no measured evidence at severe or extreme wind_cyclone; measured HARM (maladaptation) in 1 source — the practice worsened this outcome for some adopters (robust evidence, high agreement → very_high confidence; transfer: adjacent). rows.mechanism: Drought kills the trees of the system and cuts its output. Severe drought can raise tree seedling mortality by 35 to 40% because seedlings cannot match transpiration demands [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3]. In Colombia, droughts provoked by El Niño between 2015 and 2016 caused significant losses of trees planted by the project, and the area under the most recently planted intensive silvopastoral systems fell by 45 percent in the severe 2019 drought in a survey of 285 farms [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. In cabruca cocoa agroforests in southern Bahia, Brazil, cocoa tree mortality was 15% during the El Niño event against under 1% normally, 7% of the 317 woody shade trees died, and potential yield fell from 242 to 26 kg/ha, an 89% reduction, still 83% lower nine months after the drought ended [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. In Ghana, leguminous shade trees competed with the crop for soil water during severe drought, enhancing crop mortality compared with full sun [ev_tree_canopy_cover_ipccar6ch5_3].
rows.conditionality: Seedling and young-system losses dominate: the Colombian source notes established systems were more drought-resilient than traditional pastures while young ones are vulnerable in their initial years [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4], and one cited study found drought did not increase seedling mortality, though growth was impaired [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_4]. The Bahia cocoa losses carry no unshaded comparator, so they show the damage to the asset, not whether shade made it worse or better [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. The Ghana unit is the IPCC chapter's second-hand reading; the chapter writes coffee but the cited study is on cocoa [ev_tree_canopy_cover_ipccar6ch5_3]. The cocoa units are crop-specific and enter the row under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling. Brazil and Colombia are upper-middle income and Ghana lower-middle income, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4, ev_tree_canopy_cover_ipccar6ch5_3].

WOCAT compilers judged assisted natural regeneration of degraded land in Burkina Faso to cope well with general river flood, and FMNR in Kenya to cope moderately with flash flood [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood].
rows.conditionality: The literature units are a tropics review reading earlier studies second-hand; the erosion statement is forward-looking and concerns the system's soil rather than its trees, and the cacao mortality finding is the least robust grade in the review's own scheme [ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_13, ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_6]. A coconut review from Kerala, India, reports second-hand that the coconut palm withstands typhoons and flooding, a no-damage finding for that crop [ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2]. The coping ratings are practitioner judgements on technology sheets, not measured damage [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood]. Burkina Faso is low income and Kenya and India lower-middle income [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood, ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2].

rows.mechanism: Trees kept in or added to farmland hold more species than the treeless land use they replace. Pooled over 47 publications, silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures; systems with native, unplanted trees were 36.3% above open pasture against 20.9% for planted systems, and invertebrate biodiversity in native-tree systems was 53.7% above open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. A meta-analysis of cocoa found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a review of shaded coffee and cocoa reports, second-hand, a stronger decline in total species richness from agroforestry to plantations (−46%) than from forest to agroforestry (−11%), and bird diversity between 120 and 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. In Colombia, intensive silvopastoral systems are reported, citing earlier studies, to carry four times more birds and 35% higher bird species richness than grass monocultures and 62% higher ant species richness than treeless pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]; a World Bank silvopastoral operation reported increased species richness and abundance, including many forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]; and silvopastoral projects significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Niger, FMNR adoption appears to increase tree diversity by between one and three tree species per farm [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1], and Kenyan WOCAT compilers rate plant, habitat and animal diversity as increased on FMNR sites compared with degraded sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity]. Farmers in Colombia and Costa Rica see live fences as corridors for fauna and flora [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6].
rows.conditionality: The gains are measured against degraded or treeless baselines (open pasture, monoculture, degraded sites). Against native forest, silvopasture with native trees held 18.1% lower biodiversity, which marks a ceiling rather than a loss caused by the practice [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12], and the invertebrate-abundance response in native-tree systems was not statistically significant [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10]. The harm finding in this row is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while yields of about 750 kg/ha were possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Design and species matter: a review notes the benefit depends on the variety, abundance and ecological suitability of the tree species used [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3], and among coffee certification schemes in Nicaragua C.A.F.E. Practices was the only one with a negative impact on tree diversity while the others were positive [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. Several units are second-hand readings or practitioner ratings, the deforestation finding gives a direction with no size and counts as a component of biodiversity rather than a measure of it, and the silvopasture meta-analysis does not name its study countries [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6, ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. Coffee and cocoa units are crop-specific; the low- and lower-middle-income fit rests on Niger, Kenya, Nicaragua, Cameroon and the cocoa meta-analysis's mainly lower-middle-income studies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1].

rows.mechanism: Trees added to cropland and pasture store carbon in their biomass and raise soil carbon. IPCC assessments state that agroforestry accumulates between 0.59 and 6.24 t ha–1 yr–1 of carbon above-ground at field scale, with below-ground carbon often 25% or more of the gains, and describe large mitigation benefits from increasing carbon sinks in vegetation and soils [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6ch5_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccsrccl6_1]. Meta-analyses report more soil organic carbon under agroforestry than under controls or crop monocultures in sub-Saharan Africa (RR 1.2), the tropics (overall effect size 1.21) and West African fields with shrubs and trees (+ 20 to 75%) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1]; a global synthesis for IPCC Tier 1 coefficients found a mean stock change factor of 1.25 for croplands converted to agroforestry [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_1]. East African agroforestry systems stock an average of 24.2 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 Mg C ha−1 in the soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muthuri23_1]. In shaded tree crops, total biomass carbon in cocoa agroforestry is on average 2.5 times higher than in a monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1], a coffee agroforestry farm in Costa Rica stored a mean 3.6 t C/ha/yr over eight years of eddy-covariance measurement [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5], and shaded coffee plots held 29,8 Mg ha-1 more above-ground biomass carbon than full-sun plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. In Costa Rican silvopasture, carbon storage potential was 1.2 to 4.5 Mg ha-1 yr-1 against less than 1 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in pastures without trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. In Ethiopia, regeneration projects at Humbo and Soddo report 181,650 and 94,817 tonnes of CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_12], and WOCAT practitioner ratings record FMNR in Kenya sequestering carbon in biomass and raising soil organic matter, with a large soil organic matter gain rated in Burkina Faso [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_507_2019_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1358_2017_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C]. Avoided deforestation by silvopastoral projects in Colombia, compared with control properties, enters as a forest-cover component with no carbon quantity attached [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2].
rows.conditionality: The starting land use decides the sign: converting forest to agroforestry gave a stock change factor of 0.89, a soil carbon loss and the harm finding in this row, and the soil carbon change rate for grassland converted to agroforestry (0.23 t C ha−1 yr−1) was not significantly different from zero [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_3]. Measured on-farm comparisons also sit close to no effect in places: soil organic C did not differ significantly under and outside Faidherbia albida canopies in Ethiopia [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1]; in Malawi soil C under a Tephrosia intercrop was 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize, a trend with P value = 0.10 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]; the cocoa meta-analysis found no significant differences in soil chemical properties between agroforestry and monoculture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1]; and certified shade coffee in Nicaragua had positive but not statistically significant impacts on above-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_castle21s_1]. Much of the rest is assessment-level or modelled (global technical and economic potentials, per-hectare mitigation densities), and the project totals carry no per-hectare or per-year denominator [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. Only a minority of units state a size, and the pooled size rests on soil organic carbon response ratios, a component of sequestration rather than a rate; the IPCC notes regional estimates are scant and options differ by geography [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_7]. WOCAT units are compiler judgements, not measured stocks [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1358_2017_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C]. Coffee, cocoa and coconut units are crop-specific [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_kumar22_1].

A further independent source or a measured change in inequity is what is missing. The cited figures point both ways (labour and uptake gaps against women, a trial advantage for women) and are shares of households or participants, not changes caused by agroforestry [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4].

rows.mechanism: Tree shade lowers temperatures where crops and animals sit: poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, Faidherbia albida canopies lowered midday air temperature over Ethiopian wheat by up to 6°C against the open field, and reviews report shade buffering temperature effects by 2–4°C and lowering ambient temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. Shade from live fences and silvopastoral models reduces cattle heat stress, and a Brazilian comparison found 20 to 100% reductions in areas at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Associated trees buffer air and soil temperature, reduce wind and raise humidity under the canopy, and tree cover protects crops against extreme microclimate fluctuations [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9, ev_microclimate_buffering_taboada20_3, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. In a shade-by-drought experiment on cocoa in Ghana, sub-canopy temperatures were lower in shade than in full-sun plots [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. In tropical silvopasture, temperatures under tree crowns can average 2-5°C lower than outside them throughout the year, and under canopy trees averaging 20 m tall in tropical agroforestry systems temperature is about 2°C lower than at a site without trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a pan-tropical meta-analysis found mean temperature lower and daily extremes buffered in cocoa agroforestry against full-sun monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1], a coffee review reports, second-hand, that shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4], and shade reduced maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
rows.conditionality: The cell rests on proxy/component evidence (air and canopy temperature, microclimate, animal thermal comfort) rather than direct measurement of heat-stress losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. Windbreak hedges in Senegal point the other way, generally raising temperature in protected plots, so opposite signs are pooled [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. Evidence spans Ethiopia (low income), Kenya and Senegal (lower-middle), Brazil, China, Colombia, Cuba and Mexico (upper-middle) and Germany and Costa Rica (high), plus reviews with no recorded context, most of them reported second-hand, though the Ethiopian canopy temperature was measured directly on farm [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_taboada20_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. The Ghanaian cocoa shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so it captures above-ground shading only and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1]. The shelterbelt cooling is a pooled meta-analysis result from upper-middle-income China, expressed as a modest percentage change in air temperature rather than a measured heat-stress loss [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The coffee and cocoa units are crop-specific to shaded perennial systems, and two carry their source's own caveat: IPCC notes that shade trees can ameliorate rising temperatures for arabica coffee but that the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2], and the coffee review notes that in parts of East Africa excessive shade with heavy rain raised fungal infection risk [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7].
